title: About
text:
My name is Andrew Van Leuven, and my day job is as an assistant professor at the University of Vermont. My research and teaching focus on regional economics and rural development efforts that strengthen and revitalize local economies.
This site is where I share my maps. For more about me, visit my other (more professional) website.

title: The 2025 County Population Data Is Out. Here’s What It Shows.
text: Today marks the release of the latest batch of data from the U.S. Census Bureau: the 2025 County Population Totals and Components of Change. Below is a collection of a few interactive maps that visualize changes that have taken place since last year, as well as a quick guide (including code snippets) for how to load, clean, and map the data.

title: The 2025 County Population Data Is Out. Here’s What It Shows.
text:
Components of Growth and Decline
Not all population growth looks the same. A county can be growing because it has more births than deaths, because people are moving in, or—ideally—both. Conversely, decline can stem from negative natural change (more deaths than births), outmigration, or both at once. The map below classifies every U.S. county into one of four categories based on its 2024–25 natural change and net migration:









Growth Type
Natural Change
Net Migration
What it means




Growing Both Ways
Positive
Positive
Births exceed deaths and people are moving in


Migration-Dependent
Negative
Positive
More deaths than births, but in-migration offsets the loss


Birth-Dependent
Positive
Negative
Natural increase keeps the county growing despite net outmigration


Declining Both Ways
Negative
Negative
Fewer births than deaths and net outmigration—the double squeeze









Perhaps the most striking takeaway from this map is just how spatially mixed the picture is. Even in states with strong overall population growth—Texas, Florida, the Carolinas—you’ll find pockets of birth-dependent or declining counties alongside booming ones. And in states often written off as uniformly shrinking, migration is quietly propping up growth in college towns, retirement destinations, and rural amenity counties. In general, county data catches nuance that state-level summaries often miss.
Please feel free to share these maps with friends and colleagues. If you would like a particular map or data point, I am stretched pretty thin until the end of the semester but it’s still worth a try to email me at andrew.vanleuven@uvm.edu with any questions you might have.

title: The 2025 County Population Data Is Out. Here’s What It Shows.
text:
Footnotes


Much of what makes working with U.S. Census data in R so approachable is owed to Dr. Kyle Walker. His packages—tidycensus, tigris, and mapgl—have become essential tools in the applied spatial data science community. If you work with U.S. demographic or geographic data in R, his work is worth exploring.↩︎

title: Welcome to MapDork
text: This site is for “under the hood” details on maps I publish on my substack page. Below is some further detail on my “Kountry” restaurant map.

title: Welcome to MapDork
text: Interactive map

title: Welcome to MapDork
text:
Code for ggplot2 map
This code aggregates business locations into H3 hexagons at resolution 3 (approximately 4,800 square miles each), counts the number of establishments per hexagon, and clips the results to the contiguous United States. The ggplot2 visualization uses an Albers Equal Area projection and a yellow-green color scale to show the spatial distribution of businesses with “Kountry” in their name.
I use data from the YourEconomy Time Series (YTS), which covers all U.S. business establishments from 1998 to 2025. For legal reasons—i.e., it’s their data, not mine—that data is not provided in this repository.

library(arrow)
library(tidyverse)
library(janitor)
library(sf)
library(h3jsr)
library(tigris)
library(mapgl)

# Contiguous 48 states
states <- states(cb = TRUE, resolution = '20m') |>
  filter(!STUSPS %in% c("AK", "HI") & STATEFP < 60)

ytsdb <- open_dataset('data/yts')
df <- ytsdb |>
  filter(year %in% c(2021:2025), str_detect(tolower(company), 'kountry')) |>
  collect() |>
  filter(state != 'HI' & state != 'AK')

# Clean and prepare spatial data
dsf <- df |>
  mutate(longitude = ifelse(longitude > 0, longitude * -1, longitude)) |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c('longitude', 'latitude'), crs = 4326, remove = FALSE) |>
  st_transform(6350) |> # Transform to Albers
  slice(1, .by = id)

# H3 requires WGS84, so transform back temporarily
dsf <- dsf |>
  mutate(h3_index = point_to_cell(st_transform(geometry, 4326), res = 3))

# Count occurrences per hexagon
hex_counts <- dsf |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  count(h3_index, name = "count")

# Convert H3 indices to polygons
hex_sf <- hex_counts |>
  mutate(geometry = cell_to_polygon(h3_index)) |>
  st_as_sf(crs = 4326)

states <- states |> st_transform(6350) |> select(st = STUSPS)
hex_sf <- hex_sf |> st_transform(6350) |> st_intersection(states)

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = states, fill = '#FFFFE5', color = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = hex_sf, aes(fill = count), color = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = states, fill = NA, color = "black", linewidth = .15) +
  scale_fill_distiller(
    palette = 'YlGn',
    direction = 1,
    name = 'Count',
    limits = c(0, 12)
  ) +
  theme_void(base_family = 'Red Hat Display', base_size = 14) +
  labs(
    title = "Density of Business Establishments with 'Kountry' in the Name",
    subtitle = '(Each Hexagon ≈ 4,800 square miles)',
    caption = '\nSource: YourEconomy Time Series, 2025    \n'
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(face = "italic", hjust = 0.5),
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
    legend.position = 'bottom'
  ) +
  guides(
    fill = guide_colourbar(
      barheight = 0.5,
      barwidth = 12,
      title.position = "top"
    )
  )

title: Introduction to Maps
text:
Agenda

Mapping basics
Mapping in ggplot2
Data from Census and NASS QuickStats
Interactive maps with mapgl


Welcome everyone. We have about 60 minutes together, so I want to move at a steady pace through all four sections. We’ll do live demos along the way, so feel free to open RStudio and follow along. Questions are welcome at the end.

title: Introduction to Maps
text:
Packages We’ll Use Today
install.packages(c(
  "tidyverse",  # data manipulation + ggplot2
  "sf",         # spatial data in R
  "tigris",     # US Census boundary files
  "tidycensus", # Census + ACS data with geometry
  "rnassqs",    # NASS QuickStats API
  "mapgl"       # interactive web maps
))

If you’re following along, go ahead and run this now. Most of these you probably already have.

title: Introduction to Maps
text:
What Is GIS?
Geographic Information Systems = data + location

Any dataset with a spatial component can be put on a map
Agriculture is inherently spatial: counties, farms, markets, watersheds, supply chains
Maps reveal patterns that tables and charts simply cannot


Today’s goal: get you from zero to a working map pipeline in R

GIS has historically required specialized software (ArcGIS, QGIS). R has changed that dramatically. You can do most of what you’d do in ArcGIS from a .R script.

title: Introduction to Maps
text:
Types of Spatial Data


Vector data (what we’ll use today)



Type
Examples




Points
farmers markets, food hubs, farms


Lines
roads, rivers, rail corridors


Polygons
counties, states, ZIP codes




Raster data (not today)

A grid of cells, like a photo
Elevation, land cover, satellite imagery, NDVI
Handled in R via terra / stars



Almost all the data you’ll encounter in an agricultural economics context is vector data. County-level NASS stats map to polygons. Farmer market locations map to points. You will rarely need raster data unless you’re doing remote sensing work.

title: Introduction to Maps
section: What Lives in an sf Object?
text:
What Lives in an sf Object?
An sf (simple features) data frame is just a regular data frame with one extra column: geometry
Simple feature collection with 3,234 features
Geometry type: MULTIPOLYGON
CRS: NAD83 (EPSG:4269)

   GEOID  NAME         STATEFP  ALAND        geometry
1  01001  Autauga      01       1539602840   MULTIPOLYGON(...)
2  01003  Baldwin      01       4117521611   MULTIPOLYGON(...)
3  01005  Barbour      01       2291820706   MULTIPOLYGON(...)

All your normal dplyr verbs work on it. The geometry column just comes along for the ride.

This is the key insight that makes R spatial data so ergonomic. You don’t need to learn a completely new data model. filter(), mutate(), left_join() all work exactly as you’d expect.

title: Introduction to Maps
text:
Coordinate Reference Systems
The earth is round. Maps are flat. Something has to give.
A CRS defines how 3D coordinates get projected onto a 2D surface.

Three CRS you’ll actually encounter:



CRS
EPSG code
When you’ll see it




WGS84
4326
GPS coordinates, GeoJSON files, web APIs


NAD83
4269
TIGER/Line files, US government data


Albers Equal Area
5070
National-scale thematic maps





Rule of thumb: for any map showing the whole contiguous US, reproject to Albers (EPSG 5070).

The most common beginner mistake is mixing CRS. If your layers don’t line up, 9 times out of 10 it’s a CRS mismatch. sf will warn you, but always check. The other mistake is leaving Alaska in its native projection, which ends up way too far to the right.

title: Introduction to Maps
text:
Why Projections Matter


No projection (WGS84 / lat-lon)

States look stretched east-west
Distances and areas are distorted
Fine for quick checks, not for presentation


Albers Equal Area (EPSG 5070)

Shapes look familiar
Areas are preserved (critical for choropleth maps)
The standard for US national maps




“Equal area” projections are especially important for choropleths. If you don’t use one, large counties will visually dominate the map regardless of the data values.

title: Introduction to Maps
text:
Types of Maps








Map type
Best for
Watch out for




Choropleth
Rates, percentages, densities
Raw counts favor large areas


Dot / point
Individual locations
Overplotting at high density


Proportional symbol
Totals, counts by location
Symbol overlap in dense areas


Reference / base
Context, navigation
Adding too much detail




For local food data: choropleths (county-level rates/shares) and point maps (market/hub locations) will cover the majority of your needs.

One of the most common mapping mistakes I see in academic work: mapping raw counts on a choropleth. If Wyoming has 10 SNAP households, that looks tiny compared to Cook County (Chicago) with 300,000. But Wyoming also has far fewer total households. Always normalize. Show rates, shares, or densities—not raw numbers—unless you’re specifically making a point about total volume.

title: Introduction to Maps
text:
The Building Blocks

library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(tigris)

options(tigris_use_cache = TRUE)


tidyverse: data manipulation + ggplot2
sf: spatial data as data frames
tigris: US Census TIGER/Line boundaries, straight into R


tigris_use_cache is important: it saves files locally so you don’t re-download them every time you render.

title: Introduction to Maps
text:
Getting Boundary Data

# State boundaries
states_sf <- states(cb = TRUE, resolution = "20m") |>
  filter(!STUSPS %in% c("AK", "HI", "PR", "VI", "GU", "AS", "MP"))

# County boundaries
counties_sf <- counties(cb = TRUE, resolution = "20m") |>
  filter(!STATEFP %in% c("02", "15", "72", "78", "66", "60", "69"))


cb = TRUE: simplified cartographic boundary (smaller file, better for maps)
resolution = "20m": 1:20,000,000 scale (good for national maps)
The filter removes Alaska, Hawaii, and territories


There are also more detailed options: resolution = “5m” and “500k”. For a full-country map you almost never need anything finer than “20m”. Also note: tigris has many other geographies (tracts, block groups, places, school districts, congressional districts, ZIP codes, etc.).

title: Introduction to Maps
text:
Your First Map

ggplot(states_sf) +
  geom_sf()


That’s the whole thing. geom_sf() reads the geometry column and draws the shapes.

[Run this live.] Notice it looks weird: the projection is off. States look stretched. Let’s fix that next.

title: Introduction to Maps
text:
Applying a Projection

ggplot(states_sf) +
  geom_sf() +
  coord_sf(crs = 5070)

coord_sf() reprojects the visualization without modifying your data.

Compare: - No coord_sf() → lat-lon, states look stretched east-west - coord_sf(crs = 5070) → Albers Equal Area, looks like a US atlas

[Run this live, showing before and after.] The difference is dramatic. This is the single most impactful improvement you can make to a US national map.

title: Introduction to Maps
text:
Making It Look Nice

ggplot(states_sf) +
  geom_sf(
    fill  = "white",
    color = "gray40",
    linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  coord_sf(crs = 5070) +
  theme_void()


fill: interior color
color: border color
linewidth: border thickness
theme_void(): removes axes, gridlines, background


theme_void() is almost always what you want for a finished map. theme_minimal() works too if you want a subtle grid.

title: Introduction to Maps
text:
Adding Data: The Choropleth

ggplot(counties_sf) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = ALAND), color = NA) +
  coord_sf(crs = 5070) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Land area") +
  theme_void()


aes(fill = ALAND): map the land area variable to fill color
color = NA: drop county borders (they clutter national maps)
scale_fill_viridis_c(): perceptually uniform, colorblind-safe


The fill aesthetic works the same way as in any other ggplot.

[Run this live.] ALAND is the land area column that comes with tigris counties, useful for this demo because we don’t need to load any external data. In your actual work, you’ll join your own data to counties_sf, then map one of those columns.

title: Introduction to Maps
section: Joining Your Data to a Map
text:
Joining Your Data to a Map

my_data <- read_csv("local_food_data.csv")  # has a column called GEOID

county_map <- counties_sf |>
  left_join(my_data, by = "GEOID")

ggplot(county_map) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = local_food_sales_per_farm), color = NA) +
  coord_sf(crs = 5070) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(labels = scales::dollar) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(title = "Local Food Sales per Farm by County")

The GEOID is a 5-character FIPS code: 2-digit state + 3-digit county.

This is the workflow you’ll use for your challenge data. Get county boundaries from tigris, join your data on GEOID, then map it. The key is making sure your GEOID column is formatted correctly: zero-padded, character type, not numeric.

title: Introduction to Maps
text:
Choosing a Color Scale

# Perceptually uniform (good default)
scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma")

# ColorBrewer sequential
scale_fill_distiller(palette = "YlOrRd", direction = 1)

# Diverging: good when data has a meaningful midpoint (e.g., above/below zero)
scale_fill_distiller(palette = "RdBu", direction = 1)

# When data is right-skewed, transform the scale
scale_fill_viridis_c(trans = "log10", labels = scales::comma)



Avoid rainbow palettes (rainbow(), jet). They are not perceptually uniform and can create false visual boundaries in your data.


ColorBrewer (RColorBrewer package, or built into ggplot via scale_fill_distiller) was designed specifically for maps. The palettes are proven to work across different display conditions and are accessible to colorblind viewers.

title: Introduction to Maps
text:
Adding a Second Layer

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = county_map,
          aes(fill = local_food_sales_per_farm),
          color = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = states_sf,
          fill  = NA,
          color = "white",
          linewidth = 0.4) +
  coord_sf(crs = 5070) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(labels = scales::dollar) +
  theme_void()

State outlines on top of county fill = clean, readable national map.

This two-layer trick is standard for national maps. The county choropleth is the bottom layer; the state outlines float on top in white so they’re visible but not intrusive. Notice we moved the data argument into each geom_sf() call rather than ggplot(), which lets us use different datasets per layer.

title: Introduction to Maps
text:
tidycensus
tidycensus by Kyle Walker pulls Census Bureau data directly into R, with geometry attached.

library(tidycensus)

# One-time setup (get a free key at api.census.gov/data/key_signup.html)
census_api_key("YOUR_KEY_HERE", install = TRUE)

Covers: - Decennial Census (2000, 2010, 2020) - American Community Survey (ACS 1-year and 5-year) - Agricultural data via the Census of Agriculture

The API key is free and instant. Go to api.census.gov, fill out the form, get an email. You only need to install it once; it saves to your .Renviron file.

title: Introduction to Maps
text:
Finding the Right Variable

# Browse available variables
v22 <- load_variables(2022, "acs5", cache = TRUE)

# Search for what you want
v22 |>
  filter(str_detect(label, regex("snap|food stamp", ignore_case = TRUE))) |>
  select(name, label, concept)


There are ~27,000 ACS 5-year variables. load_variables() + filter() is how you find what you need.

The Census variable naming is… not intuitive. B22003_002 means something if you know the codebook, but you’d never guess it. load_variables() gives you a searchable table. I usually do str_detect() searches on the label column.

title: Introduction to Maps
Introduction to Maps
text:
Mapping the Result

ggplot(snap_rate) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = snap_pct), color = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = states_sf, fill = NA,
          color = "white", linewidth = 0.4) +
  coord_sf(crs = 5070) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    name   = "Share of households\nreceiving SNAP",
    labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1),
    option = "magma"
  ) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(title = "SNAP Participation by County (2022 ACS)")


[Run this live.] This is a complete, publication-ready map in about 20 lines of code including the data pull. Note how we normalize: we’re showing the SNAP rate, not the raw count. This is essential for a choropleth of counties that vary dramatically in population.

title: Introduction to Maps
text:
NASS QuickStats: rnassqs
NASS QuickStats is the USDA’s public database for agricultural statistics: crops, livestock, farm economics, farm counts, and more.

library(rnassqs)

# One-time setup per session (get a free key at quickstats.nass.usda.gov/api)
nassqs_auth("YOUR_API_KEY")


Covers: most Census of Agriculture tables + annual/quarterly survey data
Geographic levels: national, state, district, county, watershed

NASS QuickStats is the programmatic interface to the same data you’d find on the NASS website. For the challenge, you’re probably already familiar with some of these datasets. rnassqs wraps the API and returns clean data frames.

title: Introduction to Maps
text:
Querying NASS Data

params <- list(
  commodity_desc    = "VEGETABLES",
  statisticcat_desc = "SALES",
  unit_desc         = "$",
  domain_desc       = "TOTAL",
  agg_level_desc    = "COUNTY",
  year              = 2022
)

veg_sales <- nassqs(params)


Use the QuickStats web interface to explore variables and build your query, then translate it to rnassqs parameters.

The parameter names map directly to the column names in the QuickStats web interface. I always prototype queries on the website first, then translate them to code. The website also shows you how many records your query will return (the API has a 50,000-row limit per call).

title: Introduction to Maps
section: Joining NASS Data to a Map

title: Introduction to Maps
text:
Mapping the NASS Result

ggplot(county_veg) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = value_numeric), color = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = states_sf, fill = NA,
          color = "white", linewidth = 0.4) +
  coord_sf(crs = 5070) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    name   = "Vegetable sales ($)",
    labels = scales::dollar_format(scale = 1e-6, suffix = "M"),
    trans  = "log10",
    na.value = "gray90"
  ) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(title = "County-Level Vegetable Sales (2022 Census of Ag)",
       caption = "Source: USDA NASS QuickStats. Suppressed counties shown in gray.")


Two things to point out: trans = “log10” is important here because farm sales data is extremely right-skewed. Without the log transform, everything except a handful of California counties will be the same color. Also note na.value = “gray90” for suppressed counties, and acknowledging suppression in the caption.

title: Introduction to Maps
text:
Why Go Interactive?
Static maps are great for publications and reports. Interactive maps let viewers:

Zoom in to their own county or region
Hover to see exact values
Toggle between multiple data layers
Explore on their own terms


For a data challenge or a Shiny app, interactive maps dramatically increase engagement.

The tradeoff is file size and rendering. A ggplot map is a static image: tiny, fast, universally portable. An interactive mapgl map is an HTML widget that needs to load JavaScript and tiles. For a Quarto document or webpage, that’s totally fine. For a PDF or Word doc, stick to ggplot.

title: Introduction to Maps
text:
The mapgl Package
mapgl brings MapLibre GL into R: fast, vector-tile-based interactive maps

library(mapgl)

The core workflow mirrors what we’ve done in ggplot:



ggplot2
mapgl




ggplot()
maplibre()


geom_sf(aes(fill = ...))
add_fill_layer()


geom_sf(data = points)
add_circle_layer()


scale_fill_viridis_c()
interpolate() inside fill_color




mapgl was written by Kyle Walker, same author as tidycensus. It’s designed to work naturally with sf objects and tidyverse data. You can pass any sf data frame directly as the source argument.

title: Introduction to Maps
text:
An Interactive Choropleth

us48 <- filter(states_sf, !STUSPS %in% c("AK", "HI"))

maplibre(bounds = us48, style = carto_style("positron")) |>
  add_fill_layer(
    id     = "snap_counties",
    source = snap_rate,
    fill_color = interpolate(
      column    = "snap_pct",
      values    = c(0, 0.15, 0.40),
      stops     = RColorBrewer::brewer.pal(3, "YlOrRd"),
      na_color  = "lightgrey"
    ),
    fill_opacity = 0.85,
    tooltip      = "NAME"
  )


[Run this live.] Notice the immediate similarity to the ggplot code. interpolate() is mapgl’s equivalent of scale_fill_viridis_c(): you provide breakpoints (values) and colors (stops). The tooltip argument names the column that shows on hover.

title: Introduction to Maps
text:
Adding Point Layers

maplibre(bounds = us48, style = carto_style("positron")) |>
  add_fill_layer(
    id     = "snap_counties",
    source = snap_rate,
    fill_color = interpolate(
      column   = "snap_pct",
      values   = c(0, 0.15, 0.40),
      stops    = RColorBrewer::brewer.pal(3, "YlOrRd"),
      na_color = "lightgrey"
    ),
    fill_opacity = 0.7
  ) |>
  add_circle_layer(
    id     = "markets",
    source = farmers_markets_sf,   # your point data
    circle_color  = "#2c5f2e",
    circle_radius = 5,
    circle_stroke_color = "white",
    circle_stroke_width = 1,
    tooltip = "market_name"
  )


Layering in mapgl works the same as ggplot: pipe additional layers on top. Layers are drawn in order: the first add_ call is the bottom layer. Here we’re showing county SNAP rates as the choropleth background, with farmers market locations plotted on top.

title: Introduction to Maps
text:
Putting It All Together
A complete interactive map combining everything we’ve covered:

County-level local food data from NASS (choropleth)
State outlines for reference (line layer)
Farmers market or food hub locations (point layer)
Hover tooltips on both polygon and point layers
A legend


This is the kind of map that makes a data challenge submission stand out.

We’re going to build this together now. [Switch to RStudio for live demo using the challenge data.]

title: Putting Farm Credit Branches on the Map
text:
Photo by Taylor Siebert on Unsplash.
The Farm Credit System (FCS) is a nationwide network of borrower-owned lending cooperatives created by Congress in 1916 to ensure that farmers, ranchers, and rural residents have reliable access to credit.1 Today the FCS operates through roughly 60 regional lenders, each serving a defined geographic territory.2 As of 2021, the system held 45 percent of all U.S. farm sector debt, more than any other lender category in the country.3 The whole network is regulated and examined by the Farm Credit Administration (FCA), a federal agency established “to ensure that Farm Credit System institutions…are safe, sound, and dependable sources of credit.”4
Fair warning before diving in: I am a regional economist and not an ag finance scholar! My interest in Farm Credit grows out of some ongoing work on “bank deserts” and the downstream economic consequences that follow. In that research, we have tried to incorporate credit unions and Farm Credit associations alongside FDIC-regulated branches. The problem is that unlike FDIC and NCUA data, which are freely available and well-structured, the geographic locations of Farm Credit branches and headquarters are surprisingly difficult to pin down.
Back in 2022, I cobbled together a time-consuming method to collect Farm Credit branch addresses, state by state. That approach worked out okay, but it isn’t something I would care to repeat. As we continue building out our research on brick-and-mortar lending access,5 I wanted a cleaner, more reproducible pipeline. And with the assistance of Claude Code, I built one!
I shared an early draft of this post with Jennifer Ifft, Kevin Kim, Joe Parcell, and Alice Roach—agricultural economists who each know far more about the Farm Credit System than I do—and their feedback sharpened the text and directly informed the What’s Next section below. I am grateful for their time and generosity.

title: Putting Farm Credit Branches on the Map
text:
Mapping the Farm Credit System
Branch office locations were scraped from the Farm Credit “Find a Lender” tool, which enables a county-level lender search. To get complete national coverage, I queried every county in every state and deduplicated the results. Headquarters addresses came from a separate source: the FCA Public Directory, which lists every chartered institution along with its official address. I scraped the detail page for each institution, parsed the address into its component fields, and fuzzy-joined the results to the Farm Credit organization names to produce a unified dataset of branch and headquarters locations across the country.

title: Putting Farm Credit Branches on the Map
text:
What’s Next
Several directions worth exploring came out of the reviewer feedback.
County service territories. Each Farm Credit lender has an officially designated set of counties where it is authorized to originate loans. The FCA Public Directory lists these territories for every institution, and mapping them would reveal something the branch-location map cannot: where multiple ACAs hold overlapping authority and compete for the same borrowers, versus where a single lender operates without competition. There is an important nuance here, though. As Joe noted, county lines are becoming a less reliable proxy for actual service area; if a borrower initiates contact, a lender can legally service that customer anywhere in the US.
Institutional complexity. The current map treats all branches as interchangeable, but the underlying institutional landscape is more varied than it appears. Making that structure legible on a map is a genuine challenge: with roughly 55 associations, color alone cannot do the work, and even a well-designed association-level visualization would require careful handling of entities that appear independent on paper but operate as one. Farm Credit Services of America, Frontier Farm Credit, and AgCountry share a single board and leadership team; their Manhattan, KS and Fargo, ND offices function as branches in practice, even though the FCA classifies them as headquarters. A different, less consolidated arrangement exists under AgVantis, which pools back-office services across six associations without yet merging governance.
Branch granularity and map density. Jenny pointed out that not all “branches” are equivalent: in Kansas, some locations are outposts, open only a few days a week, which creates a different access picture than a full-service branch. It may be possible to recover this distinction from the FCA web tool. She also noted that the size of the plotted points gives an impression of a denser network than actually exists; overlaying county boundaries would help ground the map in the vast rural territories each office is meant to serve.
